magen-avraham/4:ד: Concern lest, etc. Shach wrote, and it appears Rashba follows his reason that it returns and revives on Pesach; but for us it is permitted through sixty, as Beit Chadash siman 442 seif 5 wrote, and so practice halachic decisors — end of his gloss. Requires study, for when they strained and only taste remains, according to all it does not return and revive, as in seif 3; therefore it appears Rama wrote that they removed the bread from there but did not strain until Pesach, and therefore he forbade; but if they strained before Pesach, according to all it is permitted. However, in mead that is sometimes thick there is no remedy through straining (and see Yoreh De'ah siman 84 and siman 104). Rashba wrote that one who took from that wine barrel after removing the bread from it and mixed it in other wine forbade all of it [see there]:
magen-avraham/5:ב: In water on Pesach. It implies that before Pesach one need not be stringent at all, for it is cold and water nullifies the strength of the brine; however in Yoreh De'ah siman 83 seif 5 and in Tosafot there it appears one should be stringent, for we see that goat brine is strong and water does not nullify the strength of the brine, as Maharai wrote — and this is l'chatchila; but in other salted fish one need not be stringent even l'chatchila. Darkei Moshe wrote — requires study — for perhaps if it remained in the vessel twenty-four hours it is like pickled like cooked, as in Yoreh De'ah siman 105; and perhaps since chametz before its time is permitted, we do not say pickled like cooked, as Tur wrote that cheeses do not discharge; nevertheless one may reject that we say pickled only in a moist item, not dry and hard like cheese, as appears regarding a moist item that remained in a vessel twenty-four hours; and similarly siman 451 regarding beer barrels implies one need not be concerned for this — end of his words; see there:
magen-avraham/5:ט: That they are ben yomo. Because of the stringency of chametz we do not say stam vessels are not ben yomo; and even if one says clearly to me that it was not ben yomo, it is forbidden — for a matter not placed upon people is not in their awareness — Bach, and so appears in Darkei Moshe. It implies that if one cooked it from the outset for Pesach in a vessel that is not ben yomo, it is permitted to eat on Pesach, even though lifgam is forbidden l'chatchila since one could eat it before Pesach; nevertheless this is called b'dieved — see above seif 2 and siman 451 note 21 and Yoreh De'ah siman 94 end of seif 5 and siman 95 seif 2 in the gloss; and R' Yehuda siman 1 wrote: specifically regarding a pan that Hagahot Maimoniyot is stringent about, for its custom is so all year; but regarding other vessels we say even with chametz stam they are not ben yomo (Maharik). And it appears to me Tur in Yoreh De'ah siman 122 wrote the reason we say stam vessels are not ben yomo is because it is a double doubt — perhaps they were not used today, and if used today perhaps with something that spoils b'eyna; and this in other prohibitions; but chametz — people regularly use pots, most of which do not spoil in fat, and it is one doubt; therefore forbidden. But Rashba wrote the double doubt — perhaps not used, and if used perhaps with permitted item — so chametz too can be said perhaps not used with chametz but with water or meat etc.:
magen-avraham/5:כ: One may be lenient. Because it is nat bar nat of the permitted, and furthermore stam vessel is not ben yomo; and Taz siman 442 wrote, and Maharik — some are lenient to drink mead of the whole year; but if there is concern they fermented it with beer yeast it is forbidden (see siman 442 seif 5); and all the more in places where they cook it all year in cauldrons used for burnt wine — forbidden, for it is a strong sharp item and imparts taste for enhancement in mead as is known; and if so, that it is not ben yomo does not help; and if so, forbidden to buy from gentiles lest beer became mixed in — end of his words; and see Yoreh De'ah siman 114 that one need not be concerned for yeast unless their custom is so; and see there in the gloss note 10; and what he wrote to forbid in burnt-wine cauldrons siman 122 seif 3 wrote the first sharpness does not make it for enhancement [see there]; and perhaps he holds burnt wine is sharper; requires study for practical halacha, for perhaps burnt wine can be compared to yayin nesek where not ben yomo does not help (see siman 451 note 21):
magen-avraham/8:ב: If it is not ben yomo. Although with davar charif it forbids even if not ben yomo, here since they place water on them their sharpness is nullified (Tur); and Shach in Yoreh De'ah end of seif 70 (and siman 114 seif 5) requires a majority of water [see there]; but according to Rama there it does not seem so; and it appears to me everything depends on the sight of the decisor; and if ben yomo it is forbidden, for pickled is like cooked — see seif 5; and Yoreh De'ah siman 114 and siman 96 seif 4; and in Shach there in the name of Or Zaru'a and Avodat HaKodesh regarding forbidden wine:
magen-avraham/12:_: It is not forbidden for benefit. For one did not transgress bal yeira'eh from the Torah, and there is no penalty (Ribash and Ran chapter 3; see siman 442). And it appears to me permitted even for consumption; and that he mentioned benefit is because chametz nokshah is not fit for consumption — see seif 11, for Ran in chapter 1 wrote Israelite chametz on Pesach in any amount is called davar sheyesh lo matirin and permitted even for consumption [see there]:
machatzit-hashekel/5:א: (Note 5) It is not, etc., and plainly, etc. — his intent: we say daf 76b: R' Yehudah, R' Yehoshua ben Levi — the examiner must nullify; and they challenge: why must he nullify at the time of examination — nullify it at four or five? And they answer: since it is not yet the time of its prohibition nor the time of its removal, perhaps he will forget. And they challenge: let him nullify it at the sixth hour when he is occupied burning it; and they answer: since from the sixth hour it is forbidden d'rabbanan, it is not in his possession and he cannot nullify, for R' Giddel, R' Chiyya bar R' Yehudah — one who betroths a woman from the sixth hour onward, even with Kordani wheat (which is chametz nokshah), we are not concerned for the betrothal. Rashi explained from the sixth hour and onward — from the beginning of six; and Rabbenu Tam proved that R' Giddel speaks from the end of six, i.e., the beginning of seven when chametz is forbidden from the Torah; and nevertheless he properly brings proof that it is not in his possession even at the beginning of seven when full chametz is forbidden from the Torah; and nevertheless Kordani wheat is nokshah, and he holds nokshah prohibition is only d'rabbanan; and therefore he derives full chametz from the sixth hour, whose time causes it to be d'rabbanan, from nokshah from the seventh hour onward, when full chametz is forbidden from the Torah but Kordani wheat which is nokshah is d'rabbanan. Maharil holds like Rabbenu Tam's explanation, and see the Gemara compares a matter that has leniency in itself to another matter that has this leniency from the time; therefore Maharil holds nokshah on Pesach (as Maharil holds) like Poskim that nokshah is forbidden from the Torah — nevertheless it has no karet, similar to full chametz from erev Pesach from the sixth hour onward, where one may also say this leniency that it has no karet. And this is from the time, for it is still before Pesach; and as full chametz from the sixth hour onward is nullified in sixty because it has no karet from the time — so too nokshah on Pesach, which has no karet in itself, is also nullified in sixty. That which Maharil compared chametz from the sixth hour onward which is d'rabbanan — is borrowed language, for he holds like Rabbenu Tam who explains from the seventh hour, i.e., beginning of seven when forbidden from the Torah; and Maharil who wrote from the sixth hour onward that it is d'rabbanan means from the beginning of six, for he relies on the Gemara and they are nullified at six — meaning at the beginning of six; and on this they answer since from the sixth hour it is forbidden d'rabbanan, it is not in his possession:
machatzit-hashekel/9:א: (Note 9) If it reached yad soledes bo, etc. And in Hagahot Maimoniyot end of laws of chametz he wrote: forbidden even in roasting (see note 1) — meaning, we do not rule thus, for the Gemara holds that although generally roasting forbids only a peel or kedei netilah, it implies it does not permeate more — because it does not permeate until it imparts taste, although in any case a minute amount permeates; nevertheless in other prohibitions we require actual noten ta'am, therefore in chametz which forbids in any amount the entire piece is forbidden even in roasting where a minute amount permeates throughout. But Rabbeinu Yerucham in seif 1 copied Rambam's words that wherever in other prohibitions a peel or kedei netilah suffices, likewise in chametz the law is the same — it does not permeate at all more, even a minute amount:
